The silo was one level up, in the VIEW layer. The four-line derivation `real = (1 + growth) / (1 + inflation) - 1` had been written out twice - once in RungSipRates.astro and once in growthCurve - and each copy had to be maintained by hand. A new force therefore propagated rung by rung, and whichever rung was missed went quietly wrong. The same shape produced sol-035's NaN, where a rung recomputed the contribution schedule instead of asking for it.
solution: `realRateChain(inputs, growth?)` in sipAdvice is now the ONE definition of the forces acting on a rupee - market growth, the fund's fee, inflation, and what is genuinely left - and both rungs render from it. A future cost is added there once and every surface inherits it without being touched. The sweep is additionally handed the page's own full-fidelity run so its anchor point IS the Answer's figure rather than a smaller sample of the same plan.
verification: Four tests: the two rungs report the same real rate to twelve decimals; the chain reduces to the old two-rate ratio at a zero fee; raising the fee moves both surfaces by exactly the same amount, which only holds if it is one formula; and the sweep's anchor equals the full run's figures. Live check: all four surfaces now read 6.7%, Rs 89.1 lakh before tax and Rs 82.3 lakh after.
lesson: One engine is not the same as one derivation. sol-023 said a view must never re-derive what the engine already knows, and that was read as being about big things - a ledger, a simulation. It is about four-line formulas too, and those are more dangerous precisely because they look too small to share: nobody extracts a two-line ratio, everybody retypes it, and the copies drift the first time a term is added. The test that would have caught this is not 'does each rung compute correctly' but 'do two rungs showing the same quantity agree' - which is cheap to write and is now written.

problem: The insurance analyser's whole argument - the policy's yield, whether bonds or equity can replicate it, what the frictions cost, how fragile the conclusion is - was computed by one 135-line function inside a <script> tag on a 35KB page. `runReplicationAnalysis()` read the DOM for its inputs, called `new Date()` in the middle of itself, and returned pre-formatted strings like '7.22%'. Nothing in the suite touched it. Every T5 item is a change to what that function reports, so each of them would have meant editing untested arithmetic and then arguing about the result by reading it off the screen.
diagnosis: Three faults in the same shape, all of them consequences of the code having nowhere to live but the page. (a) UNTESTABLE: inputs came from `document.getElementById`, so there was no way to call it. (b) NOT DETERMINISTIC: the XIRR's calendar started at `new Date()` read inside the function, so the policy's yield was a function of the day as well as of the contract. (c) THREE COPIES OF ONE WALK: the safe route, the growth route and the sensitivity table are the same year-by-year loop at different rates, written out inline twice and again inside a nested `getEquitySurplus()`. That is sol-038's shape exactly, and on the SIP page it printed two values for one quantity. The view had begun to grow the sol-026 fault too: the frictions panel re-read `inPremium` and `inPPT` with its own fallbacks, so the premium the analysis defaulted and the premium the GST card defaulted were two decisions that merely happened to agree.
solution: `src/utils/insuranceReplication.ts` is the engine - no DOM, no formatting, no clock. `replicate(inputs, rate, taxGains)` is the walk, written ONCE, and the two headline routes and every sensitivity row call it. `startDate` is a required input. The named assumptions that were literals in the middle of the arithmetic - 7.1%, 12%, 12.5% LTCG, the Rs 1.25 L exemption, GST at 4.5/2.25%, 20% commission - are parameters or exported constants. `src/utils/insuranceInputs.ts` is the only thing that knows a form exists, on the plannerInputs/sipInputs pattern, and it owns the cover-to-premium sync as well. The page's <script> is now a view: read, analyse, render.
verification: A throwaway parity test ran the verbatim pre-extraction function against the extracted engine over six input sets - the shipped defaults, the toggle off, a policy too generous to replicate, payouts starting inside the premium term, cover costing more than the premium, and payouts ending before the premiums do - asserting the ledger, both routes, the tax drag, the XIRR string, the frictions and every sensitivity row. All matched; the refactor moved no number. It was then deleted, and 28 permanent tests took its place in `insuranceReplication.test.ts`, including the one that says the sensitivity table's baseline row must EQUAL the headline growth figure - the assertion that makes the third copy of the walk impossible to reintroduce.
lesson: The extraction is not preparation for the work; it IS the work. Three of the four remaining T5 items are claims about the sign and the wording of figures this function produces, and none of them could be argued about until the figures could be asserted. Within an hour of the engine being callable it had already reported, in a test rather than in an argument: the safe route ends Rs 11.08 lakh SHORT at the shipped defaults while the page prints that number in emerald green under the word 'Surplus'; the bottom line calls a negative number 'SURPLUS WEALTH'; the safe route is charged no tax at all, which flatters the very route the page uses to argue the policy is beatable risk-free; the LTCG exemption is applied once to a terminal gain rather than annually; the maturity field turns a typed 0 back into Rs 10 lakh, against its own tooltip; and the walk lets an exhausted portfolio go negative and keeps compounding it, so the sensitivity table can tell a reader that a HIGHER return leaves them worse off - the deficit is worst around 11%, not at 8%. None of that was found by reading the page. All of it was found by being able to call the function.

problem: The insurance analyser's replication walk let an exhausted portfolio go NEGATIVE and kept compounding it, so a bust route grew a debt at the equity rate. The sensitivity table - whose entire purpose is 'what if returns are lower than you hope' - therefore told the reader that a HIGHER return left them worse off: on a generous policy it read 8% -> -1.73 Cr, 10% -> -1.81 Cr, 12% -> -1.81 Cr, 14% -> -1.63 Cr, worst in the middle at about 11%. Separately and because of the same negative balance, the page printed '-Rs 11.08 Lakh' in emerald green under a heading reading 'Surplus Wealth / Deficit', beside a badge saying POLICY WINS, while the bottom line called the same figure 'SURPLUS WEALTH'.
diagnosis: One fault with two faces. The walk modelled a withdrawal as arithmetic rather than as an event: `balance -= payout` with no floor. A portfolio that cannot meet a withdrawal is empty - it does not borrow at 12% and carry on - and once the balance was allowed below zero, the 'deficit' it produced was not a quantity anybody could name. That is why the labels could not be made to agree: FOUR independent decisions (heading, colour, badge, bottom line) were each reading the sign of a number that did not mean what any of them assumed. Fixing the wording without fixing the walk would have produced four consistent descriptions of a meaningless figure.
solution: The walk pays what it has: `paid = min(balance, payout)`, and what it could not pay is accumulated as `unfundedPayout` with the year it first happened, `exhaustedInYear`. The balance can never go below zero. `verdictFor(route)` then returns ONE discriminated union - surplus / exact / shortfall, each carrying its own `tone` - and the Answer, both route cards, the sensitivity table and the bottom line all render that single verdict. A route that fails now reports the two things a person actually lives through (dd-010): the year the income stopped arriving, and how much of it never came. Both are given in the rupees of the day and in today's money (T8, dd-004).
verification: Six tests. A higher return is never a worse outcome; the money lasts longer at a higher rate (year 14, 15, 16, 18 across the table); the balance is never negative at any rate from 0% to 20%; every rupee promised is either paid or counted as unfunded; across six policies x five rates a route is never simultaneously a surplus and a shortfall, and the verdict's tone follows from that one fact; and a route that misses an early payout but is refilled by later premiums still reports a shortfall, because a positive closing balance does not undo a payment the reader did not receive. Read on the live page afterwards: the same generous policy now reads 'RUNS OUT - YEAR 16' with Rs 1.06 Cr unpaid, and the sensitivity table's shortfall shrinks monotonically as returns rise.
lesson: A display bug that will not sit still is usually not a display bug. The T5 brief listed 'fix surplus/deficit labelling - sign, word and badge must agree' as a wording task, and it could not have been done as one: the figure being labelled was an artefact of a portfolio that was allowed to owe money. The general form is that a label can only be as honest as the quantity underneath it, so when four surfaces cannot be made to agree about one number, the number is the thing to look at. And the fix is structural rather than careful: there is now one verdict, so there is nothing left for the surfaces to disagree about.

problem: Two small faults with the same shape, both found by reading the live page rather than by the suite. (a) `parseFormattedNumber(field) || fallback` cannot tell 'the reader typed 0' from 'the field is empty', so typing 0 into the Terminal Maturity Benefit - whose own tooltip says 'Type 0 if there is no final bonus' - handed back a Rs 10 lakh terminal bonus the reader had explicitly said they would not receive. It inflated the policy's yield from 5.89% to 7.22% and its total payout from Rs 24 lakh to Rs 34 lakh, on a page whose entire purpose is to show that the policy is worth less than it claims. (b) `formatShortRupee` rounded to two decimals above a lakh but printed sub-lakh values raw, so the first computed rather than typed figure to reach it rendered as 'Rs 59,189.846'.
solution: `moneyAllowingZero(id, fallback)` for the fields where zero is an answer rather than an empty box - the maturity benefit and the annual income, both of which a real policy can legitimately set to nothing. A blank field still falls back; a typed zero is honoured. `formatShortRupee` rounds to whole rupees below a lakh, which fixes every caller rather than the one that showed it.
verification: Live: typing 0 into the maturity field moves the yield to 5.89% and the total paid out to Rs 24.00 lakh, and the Answer re-reads accordingly. The premium-decay line now prints Rs 59,190.
lesson: `|| fallback` is a coalescing operator being used as a validity check, and it silently swallows every falsy value the domain considers meaningful. Zero is a real answer for most money fields on a form; the test is not 'is this value truthy' but 'did the reader say anything'. Worth grepping for elsewhere. Both faults were invisible to a suite that tests the engine, because both live in the layer between the form and the engine - which is exactly the layer sol-039 created, and it needs the same reading-the-page discipline the engine no longer does.

problem: The insurance page taxed the DIY growth route on ONE number: the terminal balance above total capital invested, less a single Rs 1.25 lakh exemption. But the route funds twenty years of income by selling units, and every one of those sales realises a capital gain. Roughly Rs 34 lakh of payouts went through the fund entirely untaxed.
diagnosis: The launch gate recorded this as 'the exemption is applied once rather than annually, which OVERSTATES the tax on the DIY route, so it errs against our own argument'. That was wrong, and only implementing it showed why. Two errors pointed in opposite directions: granting one exemption instead of thirty overstated the tax by about Rs 4.5 lakh, while ignoring every gain realised on the way understated it by considerably more. The net was that the page UNDERTAXED the route it was arguing for - the opposite of the conservative direction it had been filed under.
solution: The walk now tracks a cost basis, on the SWP engine's convention (swpWorker): the gain in any sale is proportional to the unrealised gain in the fund at the time of it. Each year gets its own exemption, because that is what the law gives. Crucially the withdrawal is GROSSED UP rather than netted down - `grossUpForTax(want, gainRatio, rate, exemptionLeft)` returns how much must be sold to hand over the promised payout AFTER tax. The SWP engine takes the tax out of the paycheck, because there the paycheck is what the retiree chose to draw; here the payout is a promise, and the entire page rests on both routes paying the identical income. Netting the tax out would have quietly paid the DIY reader less than the policyholder while still calling the two comparable. Whatever survives to the final year is liquidated and taxed on the remaining exemption, because the policy's maturity benefit is handed over in cash.
verification: The gross-up is asserted exact across four payout sizes, five gain ratios and both exemption states: what the reader receives equals what was promised, to six decimals. The exemption is asserted to be granted many times, by running the same policy with and without it and showing the difference exceeds ten years' worth. Shipped figures moved: tax drag Rs 6.42 lakh -> Rs 8.38 lakh, surplus Rs 54.48 lakh -> Rs 52.52 lakh. AND A BUG WAS CAUGHT BY THE NUMBERS: the gross-up is exact in algebra but not in floating point, so `delivered` landed a fraction of a paisa under the payout and a shortfall of 1e-9 counted as a missed instalment. The engine reported a policy running out in year 12 when it ran out in year 15. It was visible only because the reported YEAR jumped around with the return rate - 14, 12, 15, 16, 14, 18 - while the total unpaid stayed perfectly monotone. Two quantities that must move together, and only one of them did. A one-rupee tolerance fixes it and the years are now 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 18.
lesson: A deferred item's own description is a hypothesis, not a finding. This one had been filed with a confident claim about which way the error pointed, and the claim survived being written into the launch gate, a solution entry and a commit message without anyone being able to check it - because until the arithmetic was implemented there was nothing to check it against. The general rule: when deferring, record what is WRONG and leave the direction and the magnitude to whoever does the work, or state them as an expectation to be tested rather than a fact. And the floating-point tolerance is the second time today that a jagged year beside a smooth total gave away a defect: two derived quantities that must move together are worth asserting together, because the disagreement is louder than either one alone.

problem: The tax calculator renders the LOSING regime as the recommended one. At 15L gross with the deductions maxed - 1.5L of 80C, 1L of 80D, 50k of 80CCD(1B), 2L of home loan interest and a 4L HRA against 5L of rent - the badge correctly reads 'OLD REGIME SAVES Rs 53,300'. Beside it, the new regime's Rs 97,500 is printed in emerald rgb(52,211,153) at font-weight 900, and the old regime's Rs 44,200 - the bill the reader should actually choose - is plain white at 700. The breakdown table's 'NEW REGIME' column header is emerald and 'OLD REGIME' is muted slate. The cards are captioned '(DEFAULT)' and '(OPTIONAL)'. So the higher tax bill is the greenest, boldest number on the page, and emerald means safe-and-recommended everywhere else on this site.
diagnosis: The styling is static and the verdict is computed, so the two can only agree by coincidence. Exactly one element - the badge - is driven by isNewBetter/isOldBetter. Everything else asserting a preference (font-weight, emerald, DEFAULT/OPTIONAL, the emerald column header, the emerald total row) is hard-coded in the markup and was written when the new regime was assumed to be the answer. This is sol-040's shape one page over: there the insurance analyser printed -Rs 11.08 lakh in emerald under the word 'Surplus' beside a badge reading POLICY WINS, because four independent decisions were being made about one fact. dd-007/dont-2 - do not render a hierarchy that does not exist. dd-012/dont-3 - do not ship a screen that leaves the reader confused, however correct its figures. The figures here ARE correct; the screen still points at the wrong one.
solution: FIXED in T6's answer layer, as the deferral said it would be. `verdictFor()` in `src/utils/taxAnswer.ts` returns one winner, and `applyVerdict()` on the page applies EVERY emphasis from it: the ring and border on both regime cards, the font weight and emerald on both totals, the breakdown's two column headers, the 'Cheaper for you' tag, and the Answer's own two cards. Nothing may assert a preference from a class written in the markup. The static ones are gone - the emerald border, the font-weight 900 on the new regime's figure, the emerald column header, the emerald total row - and the DEFAULT / OPTIONAL captions with them, since 'default' was a statement about the statute that had quietly become a recommendation.
verification: Found by reading the live page; fixed and re-verified the same way. Driven through the DOM at four states - defaults, an ordinary Rs 2 lakh home loan, the contrived maxed-deduction case it was first filed against, and back - asserting at each that the regime carrying the winning styling IS the regime with the lower bill. AGREE true at all four, including both cases that were broken, and it flips back. Also asserted in the suite, which is where it belongs: taxAnswer.test.ts sweeps 36 combinations of income, 80C and loan interest and requires verdict.better.totalTax <= verdict.worse.totalTax every time, plus a case with no income at all to check that a tie stays a tie rather than silently promoting the default.
lesson: A verdict computed once and presented five times by hand is five chances to disagree with itself, and the disagreement is invisible to a suite that only tests the engine - all 49 tax tests passed throughout, because the engine was right the whole time. THE SEVERITY WAS ALSO UNDERSTATED AT FILING TIME: recorded against a contrived input with every deduction maxed, it turned out to fire on a salaried reader with an ordinary Rs 2 lakh home loan. A defect's first reproduction is the one you happened to find, not the smallest one that triggers it, and reporting the trigger as the scope makes it look rarer than it is - the same shape as sol-042's confidently-wrong deferral note. The mechanism, not the intention: anything asserting a preference renders from the computed verdict.

problem: `renderDashboard` on the SWP planner destructured `initialMonthly` from the page's one input reader. `readPlannerInputs()` has never returned a field by that name - it returns `monthlyWithdrawal`. Astro does not typecheck the client `<script>` block, so `astro build` was clean, `npm run verify` was 376/376 green, and the field was simply `undefined` on every single page load with default inputs. No input was required to reproduce it: opening /swp-planner was enough.
diagnosis: One wrong word produced three defects, and only one of them could be seen. (a) `annualWithdrawal = initialMonthly * 12` was NaN, so the initial-withdrawal-rate readout printed `NaN%` and all four rows of the required-CAGR sensitivity table printed `NaN%`. (b) `checkSanity` computed the same rate, and `NaN > 6` is false - so the safe-withdrawal-rate warning, which tells a reader their plan draws above the 4-6% range, could never fire on any input. A safety check that is silently switched off is worse than one that is absent, because the page's silence reads as approval. (c) In the depletion branch, `deathYearGrossMonthly` was NaN, so `survivedMonths` became NaN, `NaN > 0` is false, and the endurance figure quietly dropped its months component - reporting '28 Years' where it meant '28 Yrs, 7 Mos'. The two silent failures both degrade to a plausible-looking output, which is why nobody caught them by looking. The year-by-year schedule masked the same undefined entirely, because it overrides its own parameter with `medianWithdrawalsArray` from the engine whenever that array has a value.
solution: The destructure aliases the real field - `const { monthlyWithdrawal: initialMonthly, ... }` - so the local name still says what it means. `checkSanity` and `chart-helpers` read `inputs.monthlyWithdrawal` directly. `createMicroCashflowChart` took `inputs: any`, which is what allowed the undefined read to pass; the planner is its only caller, so the parameter is now typed `PlannerInputs`. A dead `key !== 'initialMonthly'` guard in `syncUrlParams`, written by someone who had already half-noticed the mismatch, is gone. New detector `inputContract.test.ts` extracts the keys `readPlannerInputs` actually produces and every field the page and chart-helpers read off that object, and fails naming any field that is read but never produced. It was proved by reintroducing the bug: it fails with `- inputs.initialMonthly`.
verification: Live on the built page: the withdrawal-rate readout moved from `NaN%` to `3.2%` on defaults, the sensitivity table from four `NaN%` rows to 10.64/11.01/11.64/12.51%, and the page contains zero occurrences of NaN. Driving the entry field to Rs 1,50,000/month moves the rate to 12.0% and now raises the warning.
lesson: This is the second instance of the gate's open item 'a typed boundary between the compute host and the rungs', and the first (sol-035) was also a NaN. The pattern is not that the code was wrong; it is that the ONLY thing standing between a renamed field and a broken page was a person remembering. Everywhere the boundary is `any` - a CustomEvent detail, an `inputs: any` parameter - the compiler has been told to stop looking at exactly the seam most likely to drift. Note also which defect got noticed: the one that printed NaN on screen. The two that mattered more degraded silently into believable output, and a suite of 376 tests was green through all three. Reading the live page remains the only thing that finds this class.

problem: `checkSanity()` - the safe-withdrawal-rate and return-below-inflation warnings - was called from exactly one place, inside `triggerSimulation()`. But `triggerSimulation` is only reached from the advanced form and the Run button. Typing in the three entry fields at the top of the page goes through `RetirementAnswer`'s own debounced `recalc()`, which syncs the advanced form and dispatches a recompute without ever passing through `triggerSimulation`. So the entry layer - the surface the whole three-input contract exists to make the default - had no safety check at all.
diagnosis: Found while verifying sol-044. After fixing the NaN the warning still would not fire from the entry field, which at first looked like sol-044 being incompletely fixed; it was a second, independent defect underneath it. The two are easy to confuse because they disable the same warning. sol-044 disabled it everywhere; sol-045 disabled it on the surface most readers use.
solution: `checkSanity(inputs)` moved out of `triggerSimulation` and into `renderDashboard`, which every `swp:result` passes through no matter which surface asked for the recompute. One call site, reached by all of them - dd-013 applied to a behaviour rather than to a number.
verification: Live: typing Rs 1,50,000/month into the entry field alone now raises 'Your first-year withdrawal rate is 12.0%. This exceeds the commonly cited 4-6% safe withdrawal range...'. Before the change the same input left the warning hidden and its message empty.
lesson: dd-013 has always been read as being about numbers - two surfaces must not show different values. This is the same rule about a behaviour: two surfaces must not offer different levels of protection. A warning wired to one entry point is a warning that fires for the expert and stays silent for the beginner, which is exactly backwards. Whenever a page grows a second way in, ask not only 'do both compute the same figure' but 'does both run the same checks'.

problem: The SIP page's expert panel read `inputs.annualStepUp` in two places. `readSipInputs()` has never returned a field by that name - it returns `realStepUp`. Both sites therefore multiplied by `(1 + undefined/100)`, which is NaN, from year 2 onward. This was NOT found by looking at the page; it was found by extending sol-044's detector to a second page, which is the only reason it was found at all.
diagnosis: The consequences were far worse than sol-044's, precisely because nothing looked broken. (a) The headline 'after inflation' yield builds a 361-entry cash-flow series and hands it to `calculateXIRR`. 348 of those 361 entries were NaN. The solver did not throw and did not return NaN - it absorbed them and returned 19.07. The page printed '19.20% a year, after inflation' for a plan assuming 12% nominal growth and 6% inflation, where the truthful figure is about 4%. A reader had no way to tell: the number was confident, well-formatted, and roughly four times too high on the single figure that says whether the plan was worth it. (b) The ledger's 'Put In So Far' column was NaN in every row from year 2, visible only when protection was switched on, which is why the default page showed no NaN anywhere. Both sites also started from `inputs.monthlySip`, which is not the instalment at all when the reader is in salary mode.
solution: Both sites now call `instalmentInYear(inputs, yr)` from `sipAdvice.ts` - the same function `toEngineParams` is built from, so the instalment this page discounts and the instalment the simulation actually invests cannot drift (sol-038's lesson: two copies of one formula is one copy too many). That fixes the base and the escalation together, including salary mode. `inputContract.test.ts` now covers `sip-engine.astro` and `SipAnswer.astro` as well as the planner.
verification: Live on the built page: the after-inflation yield moved from 19.20% to 4.09%, which reconciles independently - 12% nominal less the 1.75% fund fee, deflated by 6% inflation, is about 4.0% before tax drag. With protection switched on the ledger's 'Put In So Far' column runs Rs 2,90,720 in year 1 to Rs 58,14,400 in year 20; Rs 25,000 a month is Rs 3,00,000 of cash in year one and Rs 2,90,720 once discounted, so the first row is checkable by hand.
lesson: Three lessons, and the third is the expensive one. First: `calculateXIRR` is a numerical solver, and numerical solvers do not report bad input - they converge on something. A NaN reaching a solver does not become a visible NaN; it becomes a plausible number. Second: the reason this went unseen while sol-044 was caught within minutes is that sol-044 had the good manners to print `NaN%`. Whether a defect is noticed has almost nothing to do with how serious it is. Third: the detector written for sol-044 found sol-046 on a page nobody had reported a problem with, in the same session, for no additional effort. That is the whole argument for building the mechanism rather than fixing the instance - dd-011/do-1, and the reason the gate's 'typed boundary' item should stop being deferred.

problem: Rahul's observation: the SIP calculator uses the Nifty 50 historical CAGR while the SWP planner uses a default 12%. Both pages in fact RENDER `DEFAULT_REGIME.growth` (13.3%) into their CAGR field, so at the surface they already agreed. Their input readers did not. `readPlannerInputs` fell back to `12` for growth and `15` for roughness - sol-028's original pair, the exact numbers that solution was opened to delete - and `readSipInputs` fell back to a hand-typed `13.4` and `28.4`.
diagnosis: Two faults sitting behind one symptom. (a) The fallback is reachable: `num()` returns it whenever the field is empty or unparseable, so a reader who selects the CAGR box and deletes its contents is silently switched into a different world. On the planner that moved the shipped answer from Rs 1.28 crore to Rs 59.5 lakh - a 53% cut - with an empty box and nothing on screen saying which figure was being used. (b) The SIP fallback of 13.4 had ALREADY drifted from the computed 13.3. regimePresets.ts opens by insisting a preset be computed from nifty50-annual-returns.json and never typed, because 'a preset that drifted from the data it claims to describe would be a fabricated figure wearing a factual label' - and a typed copy of that very figure was sitting one import away, already wrong in the first decimal. sol-028 fixed the visible default and left the fallback behind, which is the same shape as sol-033's second instance: the fix landed on the surface that was pointed at, not on every surface that had the fault.
solution: Both readers now derive their market fallback from `DEFAULT_REGIME` - growth and roughness together, because a regime is a pair and taking one page's growth with another's roughness assumes a world that has never existed. No typed copy of a computed figure remains in either reader. `inputContract.test.ts` gains three checks: both readers must import the regime, neither may fall back to a numeric literal for the growth or roughness fields, and the two must resolve to the same expression. Proved by reverting the planner to `12` and watching it fail with `F.ret falls back to 12` and `the two pages assume one world`.
verification: Live on the built page: clearing the CAGR field leaves the headline at Rs 1.28 crore, where before the change it fell to Rs 59.5 lakh. Both pages resolve growth to 13.3% and roughness to 28.4% from the same computation.
lesson: Rahul was right that the two pages disagreed, but not in the place the symptom pointed at - the visible defaults matched and the divergence was in the fallbacks. That is worth noting on its own: a report of an inconsistency is evidence that one exists, not a description of where. The general rule is that a DEFAULT is a claim about the world and must be derived from the record like any other figure, and a FALLBACK is a default that nobody looks at - which makes it the most likely place for a retired assumption to survive. When a solution replaces an assumption, grep for the old value rather than editing the site that raised it. sol-028's numbers lived on for a day in the one place nobody would think to read.

problem: Explicitly wrapping markdown hero images with `w-full h-auto object-cover` classes causes either severe vertical cropping (if max-h is constrained) or gigantic runaway scaling (if max-h is removed).
solution: Never wrap markdown hero images with explicit sizing containers or tailwind classes in the `.mdx` file. Rely entirely on the global `ArticleLayout.astro` which already provides `prose-img:max-h-[500px] prose-img:w-auto prose-img:object-contain` along with the correct dark mode blend filters.
impact: Guarantees hero images scale gracefully without cropping, while respecting the 500px vertical ceiling across all devices.

problem: Both engine pages statically imported html2pdf.js at the top of their client script. It is 914 KB - twenty times the rest of the page put together - and it is needed only if a reader clicks Download PDF. Every reader paid for it before the first number appeared, on the two pages we most want strangers to land on and to rank.
diagnosis: A static `import html2pdf from 'html2pdf.js'` makes the module a hard dependency of the page entry chunk, so the browser fetches it during module resolution, before any of our code runs. It is invisible in the page HTML - there is no <script> tag and no modulepreload link for it, because an ES module's static imports are followed by the loader, not listed in the markup. Counting the scripts the HTML references says 35 KB and is simply the wrong measurement; following the static import graph from those entry chunks says 960 KB. The page had the correct pattern in front of it the whole time: chart-helpers.ts already loads Chart.js with `await import("chart.js/auto")`.
solution:
Moved the import inside the click handler on both pages: `const { default: html2pdf } = await import('html2pdf.js')`. Rolldown emits it as its own chunk that nothing static points at, so it is fetched on the click and not before.

The handler was also changed from `.then()` to `try/finally`. The button label is set to 'Generating PDF...' before an await that can now reject - a failed chunk fetch on a bad connection - and without the finally the button would sit on 'Generating PDF...' for the rest of the session. That is the same permanently-stuck message sol-051 deletes from the same page, and it would have been introduced by the fix standing next to it.
verification:
Measured by following the static import graph from the entry chunks the page HTML references, before and after, on a clean build:
  swp-planner  960 KB -> 46 KB across 9 files
  sip-engine   956 KB -> 42 KB across 11 files
The entry chunk now reaches it only through a dynamic import of ./html2pdf._slNjp9l.js, never through a static `from` edge. Confirmed at runtime on the dev server: performance.getEntriesByType('resource') shows zero html2pdf requests on load. 390 tests green, no console errors on either page.
lesson:
The first measurement was wrong and agreed with the second, which is the dangerous kind of wrong. Counting the .js files named in the page HTML gave 35 KB before AND after, which looked like proof the change did nothing. Both numbers were correct and both were measuring something other than what the reader downloads. A payload check has to follow the static import graph, because that is what the module loader does.

The first attempt at a before-state was invalid in a way worth recording too: restoring the top-level import while leaving the dynamic import in the handler produced a byte-identical build, because the now-unused static binding was tree-shaken. The baseline had to revert BOTH halves. A control that silently equals the treatment should be suspected before it is believed.

problem: The planner shipped a footer strip reading 'Calculating actionable financial guidance...' that no script ever wrote to, so it said that permanently, sitting underneath a finished answer. A reader cannot distinguish a promise that is still loading from one that was never kept; they wait for it. Fourteen ids across seven pages were declared in markup and referenced by nothing anywhere in the tree.
diagnosis:
The same untyped markup/script boundary the rest of inputContract.test.ts covers, read in the other direction. Those checks ask whether every field the page READS is one its reader produces. This is the mirror: whether every handle the page OFFERS is one somebody takes. Astro does not typecheck the client <script>, so a getElementById that was renamed - or never written at all - leaves its markup behind and the build stays green.

The audit named six on swp-planner. A reference-aware scan found a seventh on the same page (`regimePresets`, whose buttons are bound by the `.regime-btn` class and `data-regime`, not by the container id) and seven more across six other pages. The audit had missed `regimePresets` because the token collides with the module name regimePresets.ts - a substring match will report a dead id as alive.
solution:
Deleted the dead footer strip on swp-planner, icon included: an info glyph beside no text is not a smaller version of the same component. Removed the other 13 id attributes and left their elements untouched.

Added a build-time wall to inputContract.test.ts: every id declared in src/pages must be referenced somewhere in src/ or public/ - by an exact quoted string literal, a #selector, or one of eleven id-pointing HTML attributes. src/tests is excluded from the corpus and comments are stripped, so neither prose nor the test’s own assertions can vouch for the id being tested. Scoped to pages, where the tree is now at zero.
verification: Live on the dev server, both pages: all 14 ids gone, every live element still present and still computing - the planner's dashboard renders 30 Years / MODERATE RISK / Rs 2.91 Cr and 'In 7025 out of 10,000 scenarios', and the SIP radiogroup still carries its 3 radios. No console errors on either page. The detector was proved able to fail by injecting a dead id into tax-code.astro; it named the file and the id. 386 -> 390 tests.
lesson:
THE PLAN SAID 'DELETE ALL SIX' AND SIX OF THE SEVEN MUST NOT BE DELETED. An unreferenced id means the HANDLE is dead, not the ELEMENT. `wowMetricBanner` is the entire lifetime-cash-flow dashboard; `sacrificeMetric1` wraps `valSacrificeTotalCash`, which the script writes on every run. Executing the instruction literally would have stripped working output off the page while closing a ticket about dead code. Exactly one of the seven - the footer strip - was an element with nothing behind it.

The failure message the test prints therefore leads with that distinction and both remedies, because the next person to meet it will read it in a hurry, and the wrong remedy is worse than the defect it is fixing.

The 21 remaining in components are deliberately NOT swept: most are section anchors (`rungFlow`, `taxAnswer`, `sipAnswerLayer`) that read as landmarks T9's deep-linking will want. Deciding that is navigation judgement rather than deletion, so it is recorded in the gate instead of guessed at here.

problem:
F-02, second pass. The calculator surface failed WCAG AA in both themes on colours nobody had a token for. swp-planner measured 21 groups / 50 failing nodes in light theme with every rung expanded at desktop width - more than the 16/36 recorded on 16 Aug, which had been measured with the ladder collapsed. The other four calculator pages had never been measured at all.

The failures were not one mistake repeated. They were four distinct kinds. (1) Tailwind STOCK colours with no token behind them: text-emerald-600 resolves to #009966 and measured 3.43:1 on its own badge tint, text-amber-600 to #E17100 at 2.95:1, and text-rose-600 to #EC003F - a pink-red that is not even the same hue as our own rose-500 #EF4444. (2) INVERTED light/dark pairs: `text-navy-400 dark:text-navy-500` puts the lighter tone on the light ground and the darker on the dark one, so it fails in BOTH themes at once - 2.56:1 light and 3.70:1 dark. 38 places had it backwards against 266 correct ones. (3) Raw hex in CSS that no class-level codemod can see. (4) An alpha modifier, text-amber-700/70, that spent exactly the headroom the token was darkened to provide, landing at 2.89:1.
diagnosis:
The gold fix of 16 Aug established the right shape - a separate text-on-light token, with the brand tone kept for rules, borders and dark-theme text - but it was applied to gold alone and only to `text-gold-*` CLASSES. It codemodded 76 usages across 24 files and still left `.badge-gold` setting `color: #B8941F`, the identical failing colour, as a literal in global.css. A codemod only ever sees what it greps for.

The three semantic colours had never been given the same treatment because they had no tokens at all: `text-emerald-600` was not our colour being misused, it was Tailwind's stock palette leaking in through a class that happened to compile. `text-slate-400` in the shared InputGroup was the same leak with a different name - a stock grey sitting beside our navy scale on every calculator's input fields.

The inverted pairs are the more interesting fault. `text-navy-400 dark:text-navy-500` is not a tone that is slightly too light; it is the two tones swapped. That is why it fails in both themes, and why counting failures in one theme understates it.
solution:
Three text-on-light tokens on the gold-700 pattern, each chosen for headroom on the TINTED ground it actually sits on rather than on white - the mistake gold-700 was already darkened to avoid. Canonical Tailwind amber-700 #B45309 clears white at 5.02:1 but lands at 4.64:1 on its own badge and would break the first time anyone deepened the tint, so --color-amber-700 is #A15C07 (4.80:1 there). --color-emerald-700 #047857 and --color-rose-700 #B91C1C likewise. The -500/-400 signal tones are unchanged and keep their jobs.

All four badge classes now reference tokens instead of literals, dark variants included. The chassis was codemodded off the stock -600s; 36 inverted navy pairs were swapped to the house pattern in 20 files; the shared InputGroup moved wholesale from stock slate to our navy; the footer's permanently-dark ground stopped being given light-theme tones; and a `dark:amber-400` typo missing its `text-` prefix - which silently did nothing, leaving light-ground amber on the dark ground - was fixed.

The footer wordmark was expected to need a WCAG 1.4.3 logotype exemption at 3.40:1. It did not. The ground under it is #0F172A, not the mid-tone it had been assumed to be, and the gold pair was simply inverted there like the navy ones: gold-500 measures 8.49:1 on that ground. It is a fix, not an exemption.
verification:
Canvas-resolved colour, alpha-composited up the ancestor chain, gradients excluded, mid-animation nodes excluded, run against the BUILT output at 1280x900 with every rung expanded. All five calculator pages plus the homepage and four trust pages: 0 failing nodes, both themes. swp-planner went 21 groups / 50 nodes to 0 with 537 text nodes laid out, which is asserted alongside the result so an empty answer cannot be mistaken for a clean one.

A negative control was planted mid-sweep - a #B8941F span on white - and the probe reported it at exactly 2.88:1, proving the zeros meant clean rather than broken.

`paletteContrast.test.ts`, 13 assertions, is the wall: it proves the -700 tokens clear 4.5:1 on every ground in use, that the signal tones still do NOT (so nobody lightens one back), that the -400s clear the dark grounds, and that no file in the swept set reaches past the tokens by class, by raw hex or by alpha modifier. 390 tests to 403.
lesson:
A codemod fixes the instances it can see; a token fixes the colour; only a test fixes the RULE. The gold pass did the first two and `.badge-gold` still shipped the failing colour as a literal.

And the browser is not a complete oracle. The static rule caught a `text-rose-500` on the planner's portfolio-depleted row that the probe could never have seen, because that row only renders when the plan runs out of money and the default inputs do not. Measurement sees the state it is in; the rule sees every branch. Both were needed, and neither would have been enough.

problem:
A fourth wrong way to measure contrast, after the three recorded on 16 Aug. Toggling the theme class and reading computed styles immediately reported swp-planner's dark theme at 99 groups / 399 failing nodes, with impossible mid-grey grounds like #6C727E and #B1B6BF - colours that appear nowhere in the palette. The true figure was 1 node.

Separately, and more quietly: the server already running on port 4321 was `astro preview`, not `astro dev`. It serves the built dist. Three rounds of edits produced byte-identical measurements before that was noticed.
diagnosis:
Same root cause as the `.reveal` fade already on the list, in a new disguise. The layout carries `transition-colors` on many elements, so adding `.dark` starts a cross-fade and reading during it samples a blend of the two themes. The impossible greys were the tell: a ground that is not in the palette is not a ground, it is a frame of an animation.

The stale-server fault is the PWA problem's twin - the launch gate already records that a service worker can pin a reader to an old build. Here there was no service worker at all; the server was simply serving a directory that no longer matched the source.
solution:
The probe injects `*,*::before,*::after{transition:none!important;animation:none!important}` before reading anything, and forces `.reveal`/`.reveal-scale` to their end state rather than waiting out the 0.7s fade. Theme is switched by toggling the class on the root with transitions already dead, which makes light and dark measurable in one page load instead of two reloads.

Measurement runs against the built output on purpose: production is where Tailwind's purge has already run, so it is the only build whose CSS is the one readers get.

The probe itself is now stored at scripts/contrast-probe.js rather than living only in a session: it is not run by node, it is pasted into the browser against the page being measured. Rebuilding it from the prose description cost most of an hour, which is the exact failure the memory protocol exists to prevent.
verification: With transitions killed, swp-planner dark went from a reported 99 groups / 399 nodes to 1, and that 1 was a real defect. Every ground in the output is now a colour that exists in the palette or a legitimate composite of two.
lesson: Three of the four wrong measurements were the same error wearing different clothes: reading the screen while it was still moving. The check that catches it is not a better tool but a question - is every ground I just measured a colour this design actually contains? A mid-grey in a navy-and-gold palette was the whole diagnosis, available for free, in the output I had already printed.

problem: F-01. The audit counted 317 pieces of type below 12px. 163 remained when this sweep started, and 95 of those were on the five calculator pages — captions, eyebrow labels, table headers and unit annotations set at 9, 10 and 11 pixels. Below 12px is not a style choice on a page a layperson reads about their own money; it is text a good proportion of readers cannot comfortably read at all, and it was being used for exactly the annotations that explain what the big numbers mean.
diagnosis: The rung components had already been migrated by the type-floor workstream, which is why its uncommitted edits kept colliding with F-02 inside src/components/Calculators and nowhere else. Nobody had carried the same convention into the page files, so the ladder read at 12/14px while the page around it still read at 9/10/11.
solution:
The convention already set in the tree, applied to the five pages: text-[11px] becomes text-sm (14px), text-[10px] becomes text-xs (12px). 95 instances. The one "text-[10px] sm:text-xs" was collapsed to a plain text-xs rather than left as a redundant pair.

The 17 text-[9px] labels were deliberately NOT converted. They are badges and eyebrow chips — CAUTIOUS/BALANCED/BOLD on the SIP page, the Greeks on the options page, the regime tags — and a 9px to 12px jump reflows the containers they sit in. That is a layout decision and it belongs to Rahul, so it is held as one batch rather than smuggled in under a mechanical sweep.
verification:
Measured in the browser at 1280x900 against the built output, all five pages: zero horizontal overflow, zero clipped or overflowing elements, and the only remaining sub-12px text is the 17 held 9px labels plus the 11px "INDIA" in the header wordmark, which is a brand lockup and was left alone.

F-02 was re-measured after the reflow, because bumping type moves layout and can expose nodes the contrast probe never laid out. tax-calculator and black-scholes both still report 0 failing nodes in both themes. The threshold itself cannot move the wrong way here: below 18.66px AA requires 4.5:1 regardless of size, so growing text only ever relaxes the bar.

One false positive worth remembering: the overflow check flagged a caption with class sr-only as clipped by 19px. That is what sr-only IS — 1px tall with overflow hidden. A layout checker must exclude it or it reports every accessible table caption as broken.
lesson:
A ratchet, not a ban. 317 pieces of sub-12px type across the tree means a flat rule would be red on work nobody has started, and a permanently red test is a disabled test. typeFloor.test.ts holds the swept files at zero, caps the held 9px batch so a deferral cannot rot into a habit, and lets the whole-tree backlog only ever fall — 163 to 68.

It also counted itself on the first run: 18 of 17, and the eighteenth was the literal inside its own regex. A test that greps the tree for a string must exclude the directory it lives in.

problem:
F-03, the third of D-2's three lint rules and the last one written. The audit counted 317 uppercase letterspaced runs and found ten all-caps strings visible in a single viewport on the insurance page. Measured per card on the live page, 10 of 23 cards were over budget.

The worst were not labels. They were whole clauses shouting: "A LOSS COSTS MORE THAN THE SAME-SIZED GAIN GIVES BACK", "TO MAKE THIS SAFER, CHANGE ONE OF THESE", "TAX, AND HOW LONG IT MUST LAST". All-caps is measurably slower to read because it destroys word shape, which is what a fluent reader actually recognises. It is a device for one thing on a screen — the label that must be found before anything else. Used everywhere it emphasises nothing and merely raises the volume of the page. This is dd-007 inverted: every visual difference must mean something, and when everything shouts, nothing does.
diagnosis:
Two structural causes, neither visible from the source alone.

First, most of the offending strings are SENTENCE CASE in the markup and uppercased by CSS. Reading the files suggested the copy was fine; only the rendered page showed the shouting. That also made the fix far cheaper than feared — removing the class restores readable sentence case without rewriting a word.

Second, the rungs used ONE eyebrow style for two different jobs: the card's own label ("Next question" / "Last question") and sub-headings inside that same card ("What it costs you", "With your numbers", "What it does not buy"). One style, two meanings, so the budget was blown by construction rather than by carelessness. The shared SectionTitle component did the same thing at section level, setting seven-word clauses in caps across 20 usages.
solution:
The rule, in the order it bites: (1) a full sentence is never all-caps — the objective one, and the one that caught the worst offenders; (2) within a card, only its own eyebrow keeps caps, and every other element wearing that style is a sub-heading that loses it; (3) headings, table headers, field labels and frame captions are sentence case at a real size.

SectionTitle became sentence case at text-sm semibold, which is the audit's own worked remedy. The rung sub-headings lost their caps and the "Next question" eyebrow kept its. Table headers lost theirs too: in a table of numbers a shouted header competes with the figures underneath, and the figures are what the reader came for. Verdict badges keep their caps — they are the sanctioned one-per-card label.

What was deliberately NOT touched: the held 9px regime chips (they belong to F-01's batch awaiting Rahul), and the three pages scheduled for their own rewrites. Sweeping tax-calculator and insurance-analyzer now would be work thrown away when they are rebuilt, so they are ratcheted by count instead of held at zero.
verification:
Measured per card in the browser against the built output at 1280x900, with every rung expanded and transitions killed. swp-planner went from 50 all-caps elements to 16, sip-engine from 26 to 19, and on both pages the count of all-caps runs longer than three words is now ZERO. Everything that remains is a wordmark, a hero eyebrow, a rung eyebrow, a verdict badge, a held 9px chip or a footer column heading — one per card, which is the budget.

Contrast was re-measured afterwards because the sweep also moved tones (SectionTitle navy-500 to navy-600, table headers likewise): swp-planner still reports 0 failing nodes in both themes across 537 laid-out text nodes.

emphasisBudget.test.ts, 5 assertions, is the ratchet: the rungs are held to the card eyebrow, no swept file sets four or more words in capitals, SectionTitle may not regain uppercase, no SectionTitle may be given a shouted title, and the five unswept pages may only ever get quieter.
lesson:
The source lied and the rendered page told the truth. Almost every shouted string was sentence case in the markup, uppercased by a class — so any audit of "our copy" that reads the files would have found nothing wrong. This is the same lesson as F-02's: the ground is only visible in the browser.

And the fix was structural, not cosmetic. The budget was blown because one style did two jobs — card label and sub-heading — so it could not be respected no matter how carefully anyone wrote copy. A rule that is impossible to follow by construction is a design defect, not a discipline problem.

Third time now that a test has caught its own source: this one matched the word "uppercase" inside the comment explaining the rule, exactly as typeFloor.test.ts counted the literal in its own regex. Any test that greps the tree for a term must strip comments and skip its own directory.

problem:
Rahul's tax-calculator sheet asks the deductions dropdown to be EXHAUSTIVE within the eligible set - dd-001/do-3, in his own words: "The dropdowns will have exhaustive sources of money & deductions category wise." The engine could price three Chapter VI-A sections. The catalogue drafted for that dropdown lists thirteen.

That gap is not a missing feature, it is a trap. A dropdown that offers 80TTB and then has nowhere to put the rupees produces a field the reader fills in and a bill that does not move - sol-041's shape, on ten sections at once, on the one screen where a reader is most likely to trust the arithmetic and least likely to check it.

The three sections it did have were each capped inline, as a `Math.min` written at the point of use. Three was liveable. Thirteen inline ceilings is sol-038's shape - one rule, many places - with a decade of Budgets ahead of it.
diagnosis:
The engine had no notion of 'a Chapter VI-A section'. It had three numbers that happened to be Chapter VI-A sections, and their ceilings lived in the expression that consumed them. Nothing could enumerate the sections, so nothing could offer them, and nothing could report on one.

Professional tax exposed the same confusion from the other side: it looks like a deduction and belongs with them on any form, but s.16(iii) takes it off SALARY, before gross total income is struck. Modelling it as Chapter VI-A would have been arithmetically wrong in exactly the way s.24(b) home loan interest was wrong before T6 moved it to its head.
solution:
`TaxInput.chapterVIA` is one map, section to rupees, and `CHAPTER_VIA_RULES` is one table holding every ceiling, every regime and every age gate. `computeChapterVIA()` returns a LINE PER SECTION - claimed, allowed, the ceiling that applied and a reason wherever a claim was cut - so the Income Computation panel can show the reader what happened to each rather than one total that silently absorbed the difference.

Four properties are load-bearing:

- A ceiling is the STATUTORY maximum, never a guess. Where the section sets none - 80E on education loan interest, 80G where the qualifying amount depends on the donee - the cap is `null` and the reader's figure stands. Inventing a ceiling understates a real deduction, which is the same class of harm as inventing one.
- A cut claim is reported, never swallowed (sol-041).
- 80TTA and 80TTB BAR rather than cap each other. A 65-year-old claiming 80TTA has not claimed too much; they have claimed under the wrong section, and the screen can now say which.
- s.80A(2)'s clamp is its own quantity. "Your 80C was cut" is a different sentence from "you did not earn enough for all of this to be worth claiming".

`professionalTax` is a separate field, deducted from salary alongside the standard deduction and HRA, old regime only.

The field ids are DERIVED from the rules table - `chapterVIAFieldId('80TTB')` - so a section added to the engine gets a field id, a change handler and a place in the input set without anyone remembering three files.
prevention:
`chapterVIA.test.ts`, 13 tests, holding the three properties that make the table safe to grow rather than the rupee arithmetic the older suite already pins: the ceiling applied is the statutory one, a cut claim is reported, and nothing s.115BAC withdrew is priced. One test asserts the lines and the total can never disagree, across a sweep - the panel prints both, and a screen whose parts do not add up breaks dd-009/do-1.

The survivor list is asserted explicitly: `expect(survivors).toEqual(['80CCD2'])`. If it grows, it grew because a Budget said so.
found_by: Reading `taxCatalogue.ts` against `TaxInput` before adopting it, rather than wiring the form first and discovering the dead fields from the screen.

problem: sol-051's dead-id wall fired on three fields that were live. Once the Chapter VI-A field ids became derived - `` `inDed${section}` `` - the wall's harvest could no longer see a holder for `inDed80C`, because the holder is a template literal and the harvest only matches a handle spelled out in full.
diagnosis: The wall was right that it could not see the holder and wrong about the fact. That is the worse of the two failure modes: a wall that fires on correct code is a wall someone eventually switches off, and then it stops catching the real ones too.
solution: The harvest now also collects CONSTRUCTED PREFIXES - the static head of any template literal of the form `` `prefix${...}` `` - and an id is held if it starts with one. The prefix must be at least four characters, so a bare `` `${x}` `` cannot admit everything and quietly turn the test green for all inputs.
prevention: Three assertions added to the existing guards-the-guard test: the widening must admit `inDed80C`, and must still refuse both of the known-dead ids the wall was built on. A widening that cannot fail is dd-011's store with no failure mode.
found_by: The suite, immediately, on the first run after the ids became derived.

problem:
`typeFloor.test.ts` was RED at HEAD and green for anyone who happened to have the type-floor workstream's uncommitted migration in their working tree. `npm run verify` passed locally on 17 Aug and the committed tree it was vouching for did not.

The numbers say it best. `BACKLOG_CEILING` was 121. The committed tree holds 213 and the working tree holds 40, so 121 was never true of either - it was a snapshot of somebody's working tree partway through a migration that then kept going. `HELD_9PX` was 20; HEAD holds 21 and the gate records 17. Three different numbers for one quantity, all of them honestly measured, none of them of the same thing.
diagnosis:
The file states the principle and then breaks it. Its comment above `SWEPT` is explicit - "a test that depends on an uncommitted working tree is not a wall, it is a coincidence" - and `SWEPT` was correctly kept to committed files for exactly that reason. The two WHOLE-TREE constants were then measured by walking the filesystem, which is the uncommitted working tree by another name.

That is the more interesting half: knowing the rule was not enough, because the rule was applied to the list of files and not to the counts. A principle stated in prose beside the code it does not govern is dd-012's shape - dd-009 and dd-010 were cited by id in the very rung that broke them.

The count being wrong for the 9px labels matters more than for the backlog: that is the number Rahul is being asked to rule on, and a deferral whose size nobody can state is a deferral that grows.
solution:
Both whole-tree counts are now read from COMMITTED content - one `git grep` against HEAD - which is the same number in every clone and every CI run regardless of what is lying around unstaged. `BACKLOG_CEILING` is 213 and `HELD_9PX` is 21, both measured at HEAD.

Raising the ceiling from 121 to 213 is not a loosening. 121 was never a figure the committed tree met; the ratchet now holds a number that is true, and 173 of the 213 fall the moment the type-floor workstream commits.

The cost is stated rather than hidden: a regression introduced in the working tree is caught by the run AFTER it is committed, not before. The `SWEPT` assertion is the immediate wall and is exact and at zero on the five pages where that latency would matter.
prevention:
A guards-the-guard test. `git grep` exits 1 on no match, which `execFileSync` raises - so ZERO, the state this ratchet exists to reach, would have ERRORED the test rather than passed it, and a measurement that fails on success is one that gets deleted the day it works. It now returns 0 and rethrows anything else, and a nonsense pattern is asserted to come back 0.

Deliberately NOT asserted: that the count still equals the ceiling. It falls the moment the other workstream commits, and a guard that fires on legitimate progress is the disease this solution is curing.
found_by: Verifying the INDEX rather than the working tree before committing sol-056 - HEAD plus the staged diff, in a throwaway worktree. 414 tests passed and the only two failures were this, failing identically at pristine HEAD.

problem:
`taxCatalogue.ts` was started in a previous session and left untracked, unverified and never run - no importers, no tests. Read against `TaxInput` before adopting it, it had one real idea and two faults.

The idea, which is kept: an exclusion is not a boolean, it is a `statute` string naming the provision that forbids the option. You cannot exclude something without saying why the law forbids it, which turns dd-020's own test - "is this removed because the statute forbids it, or because we guessed?" - into something a machine can ask.

Fault one: THIRTEEN of its options had nowhere for their rupees to go. The engine could not price them. Wiring the form to it would have produced boxes the reader fills in and a bill that does not move - sol-041, on a tax return.

Fault two: home loan interest appeared TWICE, once as a house-property income source and once as an s.24(b) deduction, both writing `houseProperty.interest`. A reader adding both would have typed one number twice and had one of them silently disregarded.
diagnosis:
The catalogue described what a reader might have without ever asking what the engine could receive. That is a natural way to draft it and a dangerous way to ship it: exhaustiveness (dd-001/do-3) reads as a licence to list everything, when what Rahul asked for is exhaustiveness within what the tool can actually DO with the answer.

The duplicate came from the same place - it is one thing in the Act, in two places in the reader's head, and modelling both views as entries meant modelling one field as two.
solution:
Every entry now names a `target`: a dotted path into the engine's `TaxInput`, or `chapterVIA.<SECTION>` for a deduction the engine holds in its map. sol-056 gave ten of the thirteen a home. The remaining two - s.115BBH on virtual digital assets and s.115BB on winnings - are marked `pending` WITH THE REASON and are not offered: both are flat rates that take no share of the basic exemption and admit no set-off, so neither can ride on the capital-gains path, which does both. Putting winnings into `otherIncome` would tax them at slab - nil for a small earner - and understating tax is the one direction this engine must never round.

The duplicate is resolved in the reader's favour: home loan interest is a DEDUCTION, which is where Rahul's sheet puts it and where a reader looks for it. The engine's house-property head is where it lands.

Several entries deliberately SHARE a target - F&O, intraday and a shop's profit all sum into `business.netProfit` - because that is what a head does. It is asserted, because a form that let the last writer win would silently drop the others.

And the catalogue no longer restates a rule the engine owns: a Chapter VI-A entry may NOT declare its own `regimes`, and takes them from `CHAPTER_VIA_RULES` instead. One rule in two places is sol-038, with a Budget every February to pull them apart.
prevention:
`taxCatalogue.test.ts`, 21 tests. The target of every offered entry is resolved against the real `EMPTY_TAX_INPUT` by walking the path, so a renamed engine field fails here rather than at runtime. Every exclusion must name a provision at length and name a category that exists. Nothing may be excluded from every category at once - that is a deletion wearing an eligibility rule's clothes. Every category must keep all five heads and more than three quarters of all sources, which catches an exclusion written one line too broadly.

dd-020/dont-3 is tested in its strongest form: `tax.ts` is asserted never to import this module, so the engine cannot consult a category even if someone wanted it to. Same facts, same tax, whatever category is chosen.

The pending queue is a ratchet - asserted to be exactly ['vda', 'winnings'], so it can only shrink. Adding an option the engine cannot price is the fault this file exists to prevent.
found_by: Reading the untracked file against the engine's TaxInput before adopting it, as the session was asked to - verify it, test it and commit it, or delete it and start over.

problem:
The safe DIY route was charged NO TAX AT ALL while the growth route paid 12.5% LTCG. Interest on a bond or an FD is taxed at slab, and the page had no income input to apply one with, so it applied none.

This was never a rounding matter. The safe route is the one the page uses to argue a policy is beatable WITHOUT taking risk, so leaving it untaxed flattered exactly the conclusion the page was already reaching. dd-021's own test names it: 'if either route is charged a tax or a fee the other is spared, the thesis has already been built into the defaults.'
diagnosis:
Two faults, and the second is the one that made this more than a missing parameter.

The first: no rate. Rahul ruled on 17 Aug that the reader supplies it - 'ask them to choose a slab. 10, 20, 30' - rather than the tool assuming one. Assuming would have put OUR number inside the reader's own comparison, and a single conservative 30% would have been the same fault pointing the other way: over-taxing DIY hands the win to the policy.

The second, and it would have produced a wrong answer even with the right rate: INTEREST IS NOT A CAPITAL GAIN. It is taxed as it accrues, every year, whether or not a rupee is withdrawn - so the tax leaves the balance annually and the money it would have compounded on is gone for good. Capital gains tax waits for a sale and compounds until then. The engine's third parameter was a BOOLEAN, `taxGains`, which could express 'taxed like equity' and 'not taxed' and had no way to say 'taxed like interest'. Charging the equity path a slab rate would have understated the drag.
solution:
`taxGains: boolean` becomes `taxation: Taxation`, a union of three modes: `capitalGains` (rate + annual exemption), `slabOnAccrual` (rate, applied to each year's growth and removed from the balance), and `none`, kept only so tests can measure what a tax costs. `PolicyInputs.slabRatePct` is a required input; `SLAB_RATES_PCT = [10, 20, 30]` and a select on the page carry Rahul's three choices.

The default is 20, the MIDDLE of the three, and that is a decision rather than a convenience: 10% flatters DIY, 30% flatters the policy, and 20 is the only one of the three that is not an argument. The control sits in the open, above the fold, with a line saying why it matters.

The reader's rate is validated against the offered set rather than coerced with `Number(v) || DEFAULT`, which is the sol-041 shape in a percentage's clothes: a renamed option would fall through to 20% and quietly retax the route this page argues for.
prevention:
Six new tests. The properties, not the rupees: a higher slab always leaves the reader worse off; taxing on ACCRUAL costs strictly more than taxing the same rate on sale (the assertion that says the two mechanics really are different); the growth route is untouched by the slab while the safe route moves; and a zero rate reproduces the untaxed walk exactly. `finalBalance` could not be used for any of these - sol-040 floors it at zero and the safe route already runs out - so they compare `finalBalance - unfundedPayout`, which stays monotone past exhaustion.

The test that recorded this defect ('leaves the safe route untaxed - which is a defect, recorded here rather than defended') was INVERTED in place rather than deleted and replaced elsewhere, so the engine's ledger of its own assumptions shows its own corrections.
impact: The shipped figures moved a long way, and they moved TOWARD THE POLICY. At the default 20% slab the safe route now runs out in year 25 rather than year 30, with Rs 17.18 lakh of promised income unpaid instead of Rs 11.08 lakh. At 30% it is year 23 and Rs 19.06 lakh. Verified on the built page, not only in tests. The tool had been biased against the product it was assessing, which is the precise failure dd-021 exists to prevent.
found_by: dd-021's test, applied to the page that entry was written about. Escalated to Rahul as an open decision on 16 Aug and answered on 17 Aug.

problem:
The tax form asked eleven questions and the catalogue held thirty-five. Rahul's brief is that the dropdowns are EXHAUSTIVE within what a category is eligible for - and the page had no dropdowns, no category, and no way for a source it did not name to reach the engine.

Building the missing twenty-four as more markup would have made the input reader wrong in a way no test could see. Several catalogue entries share one engine field ON PURPOSE, because that is what a head does: salary, pension and arrears are one figure to the slabs, and a shop's profit, F&O, intraday, freelance and gig income are one business profit. A reader that took one id per field would have written whichever arrived last and dropped the rest in silence - sol-041 with nineteen income sources behind it.
diagnosis:
Three things had to change together, and doing any one of them alone would have been worse than doing none.

FIRST, THE READER SUMS BY TARGET. `readTaxInputs()` walks the catalogue rather than a list of ids, adds every active field's rupees to the `target` it names, and assembles `TaxInput` from the totals. Entries sharing a target sum into it, which is right.

SECOND, PRESENCE STOPS MEANING ANYTHING. Every eligible field is rendered by the server, hidden until the reader adds it, so a section merely on the page must not read as claimed. `readChapterVIA()` keyed off field PRESENCE and had to move to `data-active` - and the attribute is set by the same function that shows the field, because a field on screen that reads as inactive is a box the reader fills in and a bill that does not move.

THIRD, THE LAYOUT HAS THREE INPUT BLOCKS. Rahul read back the illegible verb on sheet 2 on 17 Aug - 'only those that can't be clubbed in dropdown-1', negatively - which reversed the transcription's reading. Block 2 is not an annotation on the income dropdown; it is a separate block for what the income dropdown cannot hold.
solution:
`taxCatalogue.ts` gains `unclubbable`, and it is A REASON STRING RATHER THAN A BOOLEAN, on exactly the discipline `Exclusion.statute` already set: you cannot take a source out of the ordinary income block without saying what summing it would destroy. Six entries carry one - the four capital-gains buckets, each with its own rate, and the two presumptive elections, which take turnover and receipts rather than profit.

AND THE RULE DECIDED THE HARD CASE RATHER THAN TASTE. A source whose target is SHARED with another is clubbed by construction, because the form sums them; so 'cannot be clubbed' and 'shares a target' are contradictories, and a test asserts it. That test is what keeps futures and options in block 1 even though Rahul's sheet lists it in block 2: F&O shares `business.netProfit` with four other sources, so a heading saying it cannot be added to the figures above would be a promise the arithmetic does not keep. The separation he has in mind is real in the Act and is not one the ENGINE makes yet. On the launch gate, for him, rather than smoothed over either way.

Field ids are derived from the catalogue - `inFld_${entryId}` - so a source added there arrives with a field, a change handler and a place in the input set. `taxInputs.ts` imports `taxCatalogue.ts`, which is allowed and correct; only `tax.ts` is barred from it, and a test enforces that, because a category filter must never be able to reach the arithmetic.

A FIELD THAT BECOMES INELIGIBLE IS KEPT. Switch category and a field the reader has answered stays on screen carrying the statute that now excludes it. Deleting it would move the tax for a reason the screen never gave - dd-020/dont-3. An unanswered one goes quietly, because it moves no money and so nothing can change behind the reader's back.
prevention:
`buildTaxInput()` is split out as a pure function taking the summed targets and the handful of facts no catalogue entry owns, so a test can put a rupee on EVERY target the catalogue names and assert it arrives. sol-059's test proves each target RESOLVES against `TaxInput`; this one proves the reader DELIVERS to it, which was the half still being checked by reading.

Four more: an unclubbable entry states its reason at length; no unclubbable entry shares a target; every capital gain is in the separate block and F&O is not; both blocks are non-empty for every category. And `chapterVIA` is empty when nothing was activated, non-empty at zero when something was - the presence-to-attribute move, asserted rather than described.
impact:
The form offers 19 income sources and 16 deductions where it offered eleven fields, and every one of them reaches the engine. A salaried filer is offered futures and options and not 44AD; a business gets 44AD and not 44ADA; switching between them keeps every figure already entered.

ONE DEFECT WAS FOUND IN THE BROWSER AND IT WOULD HAVE BEEN INVISIBLE FROM THE TESTS. The kind of house property is derived from what the reader declared rather than asked as a fourth question - but it was keyed off whether the FIELD was active, and 'Rent received' is one of the few fields permanently on screen, so it is active for everybody. Every reader with a home loan was being treated as a landlord, and a let-out property's interest is uncapped where a home you live in is capped at Rs 2 lakh. It now reads the FIGURE. Presence had been smuggled back in under another name, on the one field where it looked safest.
found_by: Rahul's sheet 2, transcribed and read back before anything was built from it. The reading back is what caught it: the first transcription had block 2 as an annotation rather than a block, and building from that would have summed four capital-gains buckets into one figure and destroyed the rates.

problem:
Sheet 2 asks for TWO output panels where the page had one table: Income Computation separate from Tax Computation, so the reader follows gross income through to taxable income before any rate touches it. The sheet's own title carries it - `UI Design - Income Computation`.

The page had no way to show what happened to a claim. sol-056 built a line per Chapter VI-A section - claimed, allowed, the ceiling that applied and a reason wherever a claim was cut - and nothing on screen read them. A reader whose Rs 4 lakh of 80C became Rs 1.5 lakh was shown one deduction total that had silently absorbed the difference.
diagnosis:
Splitting the table was the easy half. The hard half is that a computation panel makes a promise the old table did not: every subtotal has to FOLLOW from the rows above it. Three places where it did not, all found by reading the built page rather than by a test:

THE GAINS BLOCK DID NOT ADD UP. The bucket rows printed `taxed` and the subtotal printed `specialRateIncome`, which is the GAIN. Rs 1,75,000 stood under a total of Rs 3,00,000 with nothing on screen to explain the gap, which is dd-009/dont-1 in the panel built to prevent it.

GROSS TOTAL INCOME WAS NOWHERE. `TaxRegimeResult` carried `grossIncome` (what the reader EARNED, the denominator of the effective rate) and `slabIncome` (what is left after Chapter VI-A) and nothing in between, so the deduction rows appeared to come off a figure that was not on screen.

AN ELECTED PRESUMPTIVE BASIS DISPLACES THE BOOKS. A reader who typed a profit of Rs 8,00,000 and elected s.44AD saw Rs 3,00,000 on the panel, with the explanation sitting in the form beside the control rather than where the difference appears.
solution:
`grossTotalIncome` is added to `TaxRegimeResult` - s.80B(5), the heads after every set-off the year allows, and the figure Chapter VI-A is applied to. Distinct from `grossIncome` and named so, because the two differ and the panel needs the second by name.

The gains rows now carry the GAIN, with what the exemptions took coming off on their own indented lines - s.112A's yearly allowance, and the part of the basic exemption the reader's other income did not use. The subtotal is then reachable from the rows.

A losses row is computed as the residual and shown only when it exists, because the set-off rules can reduce gross total income by an amount that appears in no head. Without it the column silently stops adding up.

The Chapter VI-A lines are grouped by REASON rather than printed one per section: a reader claiming 80C, 80D and 80CCD(1B) under the new regime needs to be told once that s.115BAC withdrew them, with the sections named, not three times. Grouping on the engine's own reason string means the page never has to know which reasons exist.

A row that carries no figure is absent rather than shown at nil. A surcharge row at zero tells the reader that surcharge is a thing that might happen to them and nothing else.
prevention:
The two panels' design was answered rule by rule BEFORE either was written - `TaxIncomeComputation.checks.md` and `TaxComputation.checks.md`, 37 don'ts each, two RISKs filed rather than smoothed over. Both RISKs are the same one and it is honest: a complete computation is exactly the artefact that can be arithmetically perfect and unreadable, and whether it lands is a judgement about the built page rather than a property the markup guarantees.

What the markup does guarantee is that no emphasis is written into it. `taxColNew` / `taxColOld`, the two column heads and the two total cells are handles, and every class on them is applied by the page's one `verdictFor()` - sol-043, which the split into two panels would otherwise have quietly undone by giving the winner two more places to be decided.
impact:
